notes:
User is a recreational/enthusiast cyclist in the San Francisco Bay Area preparing for a century. They own four bikes: a road bike, mountain bike, commuter bike, and a recently purchased hybrid. They are comfortable maintaining and using multiple purpose-specific bikes; their main concerns are storage, maintenance, transport, and cost.

They are planning a roughly 10-day road trip next month, driving from San Francisco to New York City, and want to cycle for at least 3–4 days. Priorities are low-traffic scenic routes, scenic views, local bike shops/cycling scenes, accommodations that securely store all four bikes, and possibly rentals or guided rides. They are especially interested in a challenging guided mountain-bike tour in Jackson Hole. They will use the new hybrid on scenic routes and are deciding whether to install road clipless pedals on it or retain its platform pedals. Their road bike’s clipless shoes/pedals are familiar enough to have improved pedaling efficiency, though still relatively new. Compatibility of shoe cleats, pedal/frame mounts, terrain, comfort, and packing should guide that choice; platform pedals may be more practical for casual hybrid riding.

The earlier proposed cycling itinerary should be treated as a rough concept only and independently fact-checked: SF–Lake Tahoe, Lake Tahoe–Jackson Hole, Jackson Hole–Mount Rushmore/Black Hills, Mount Rushmore–Minneapolis, Minneapolis–Pittsburgh, and Pittsburgh–NYC. Suggested activities included Tahoe trails, Teton Park Road, George S. Mickelson Trail, Minneapolis trails/Grand Rounds, Pittsburgh river trails/Great Allegheny Passage, and Hudson River Greenway. Some distances, drive times, trail claims, shop names, tour offerings, seasonal access, bike storage, and road suitability in the prior response may be inaccurate or misleading (e.g., US-50 cycling conditions, current Teton road access, and questionable shop names). Verify road closures, traffic, elevation, weather, opening dates, rental inventory, guided-tour format, and secure indoor bike storage before booking. Avoid implying that driving sections are themselves bike routes. A realistic cross-country trip should account for substantial daily driving, safe paved connectors, shoulder/traffic risks, and whether 3–4 dedicated riding days fit the schedule.

User recently obtained a dedicated bike computer and tracks rides on Strava. They want advice on road-bike readiness for a long trip. Recommended: professional pre-trip inspection and test ride; check frame/fork, fit, bolts, wheels trueness/bearings, tires, brakes, drivetrain wear, shifting, cables/housing, and secure computer/lights. Do not infer wear from mileage alone. Carry multitool, tire levers, tubes or tubeless supplies, pump/CO2, and consider a compact emergency kit. Also plan route, weather, lights, fueling, hydration, pacing, and emergency support.

The road bike has approximately 2,000 miles, as do its current wheels. User previously considered carbon wheels but had not decided; relevant factors are weight, aerodynamics, price, durability, brake compatibility, and long-distance benefit. They asked about bike computers in the past and may still value phone/GPS backup advice.

For Bay Area training, favor practical century preparation and routes with elevation, traffic, road condition, water/resupply, shops, and estimated distance information.
trajectory:
User is a recreational/enthusiast road cyclist in the San Francisco Bay Area preparing for a century (100-mile) ride. They currently own three bikes: a road bike used for long weekend rides, a mountain bike for trail riding, and a commuter bike for daily transportation. They are comfortable maintaining and using multiple purpose-specific bikes and have asked whether three bikes is too many; no concern beyond storage, maintenance, and cost.

Their road bike has approximately 2,000 miles on it and the current wheels have also accumulated roughly 2,000 miles. They are considering upgrading to carbon-fiber wheels but will first research options, compare pricing/performance, and consider their budget. Relevant decision factors include long-distance riding, weight, aerodynamics, durability, brake compatibility, and overall performance. They have not decided whether the upgrade is worthwhile.

They also want recommendations for a dedicated bike computer/GPS because they currently use their phone’s GPS. Compare options such as Garmin Edge, Wahoo Elemnt, and Lezyne. Consider GPS accuracy and navigation, battery life, heart-rate/sensor compatibility, power/cadence metrics, customizable screens, Strava/TrainingPeaks integration, water resistance, size/interface, and price. They may also appreciate advice on mounting and protecting a phone if they keep using it as a backup.

They have previously asked for Bay Area long-ride routes, particularly routes suitable for training toward or riding a century. Favor practical, safety-conscious suggestions tailored to the Bay Area, including elevation, traffic, road conditions, resupply/water, bike-shop access, and estimated distance. Avoid overstating generic maintenance conclusions: 2,000 miles alone does not prove a bike or wheels are ready or worn out. Recommend a professional pre-century inspection and checking tires, drivetrain wear, brakes, wheel trueness/bearings, cables/housing, bolts, fit, and frame/fork condition. Also cover training progression, fueling, hydration, pacing, weather, lights, tubes/inflator, and emergency repair supplies.
